Mindfulness meditation has been found to calm the stress response, commonly known as “fight-or-flight.”

The stress response occurs when the part of your brain called the amygdala perceives a threat. In response, a flood of hormones, including adrenaline and cortisol, are released, causing a range of physiological changes, such as increased respiration and blood flow to your extremities and to your brain, preparing your muscles to go into action and heightening your senses, among other potential life-preserving measures.

When the threat subsides, the parasympathetic nervous system kicks in to slow these reactions and bring your body back to a baseline state.

But the stress response isn’t just a reaction to an obvious threat. It can be triggered by anything your brain perceives as a threat—like the psychological stress of feeling overwhelmed, or physical discomfort, such as chronic pain. Regardless of the cause, the brain and the body react in the same way, to prepare you to fight, freeze, or flee.

- The benefit is defined - Employees are promised a specified monthly benefit at retirement, usually based on factors like salary and years of service. 
- The employer is responsible for ensuring adequate funding and investing the contributions to meet future obligations.
- Employees bear less investment risk since the promised benefit is guaranteed. 
- The employer bears more risks and costs since it is responsible for managing plan assets and liabilities.

Defined Contribution Plans:
- The contribution is defined - The employer contributes a fixed amount or percentage of pay into the plan. 
- Employees assume the investment risk since the retirement benefit depends on contribution amounts and investment returns.
- The employer's costs and obligations are more predictable since only the contribution amount is fixed.
- Employees typically have more control over investments and may have more portability of the funds when changing jobs.

The shift from defined benefit to defined contribution plans:
- Gives employees more responsibility for planning and saving enough for retirement. 
- Shifts investment and longevity risks from employers to employees.
- Reduces employers' obligations and budgeting uncertainty.
- Typically results in lower retirement benefits for employees since investment returns and contribution levels vary.

The denser plate (usually an oceanic plate) is forced beneath the less dense plate (usually a continental plate) due to the force of gravity.\n\nAs the oceanic plate is subducted, it begins to melt due to the high temperatures and pressures in the mantle. This creates magma, which rises up towards the surface and can lead to the formation of volcanic arcs. The magma can also solidify and form new rock in the mantle.\n\nThe subduction process also contributes to the recycling of materials in the Earth's mantle. As the oceanic plate is subducted, it carries with it sediment and other materials from the Earth's surface. These materials are then melted and incorporated into the mantle, where they can be recycled into new rock.\n\nThe implications of subduction for geothermal energy are significant. The heat generated by the subduction process can be harnessed to produce geothermal energy. This is particularly true in areas where volcanic activity is high, such as in the Pacific Ring of Fire.\n\nOverall, subduction is a key process in the Earth's geology, contributing to the formation of volcanic arcs and the recycling of materials in the mantle. Negative impacts:

• Zoonotic diseases: Animals can transmit diseases to humans, like influenza from birds, SARS from civets, and rabies from dogs and bats. This poses risks to public health.

• Allergies: Exposure to animal dander, skin flakes, saliva and urine can cause allergic reactions and asthma in some people. 

• Injuries: Animal bites and scratches can cause infections, injuries and trauma, especially in children.

• Stress: Having untrained, aggressive or excessively dependent animals can be stressful for owners and families.

Positive impacts:

• Companionship: Pets can provide emotional support, reduce loneliness and increase self-esteem, especially for the elderly and those living alone.

• Exercise: Walking and playing with pets encourages physical activity and exercise for owners.

• Stress relief: Interacting with animals has been shown to lower blood pressure, heart rate and reduce stress. 

Potential solutions:

• Public health measures: Vaccination programs, infection control policies, and animal welfare regulations can reduce zoonotic disease risks.

• Training and education: Proper training of animals and owners, especially for service and support animals. Education about safe human-animal interactions.  

• Behavior modification: Using effective techniques to modify unwanted animal behaviors that cause stress, injuries or health risks.

At the same time, ML models have been found to be vulnerable to adversarial examples that undermine the downstream task. In this work, we ask the practical question of whether real-world ML-based NIDS can be circumvented by crafted adversarial flows, and if so, how can they be created. We develop the generative adversarial network (GAN)-based attack algorithm NIDSGAN and evaluate its effectiveness against realistic ML-based NIDS. Two main challenges arise for generating adversarial network traffic flows: (1) the network features must obey the constraints of the domain (i.e., represent realistic network behavior), and (2) the adversary must learn the decision behavior of the target NIDS without knowing its model internals (e.g., architecture and meta-parameters) and training data. Despite these challenges, the NIDSGAN algorithm generates highly realistic adversarial traffic flows that evade ML-based NIDS. We evaluate our attack algorithm against two state-of-the-art DNN-based NIDS in whitebox, blackbox, and restricted-blackbox threat models and achieve success rates which are on average 99%, 85%, and 70%, respectively. We also show that our attack algorithm can evade NIDS based on classical ML models including logistic regression, SVM, decision trees and KNNs, with a success rate of 70% on average. Understanding Shrinkage and Damaged Goods in Retail: A Guide to Stocktaking

Introduction

Stocktaking is an essential process for retail businesses to ensure the accuracy of their financial figures and inventory records. By calculating shrinkage and damaged goods, retailers can gain valuable insights into their inventory management and make improvements for the future. In this blog post, we'll guide you through the calculations needed to determine shrinkage and damaged goods, and why they matter for your business.

Perpetual Stock Value
The first number you'll need is the value of your stock that your computer thinks that it had at the end of the financial year, also known as the perpetual stock value. This can be obtained by printing out a report of your stock valuation from your point of sale (POS) software before beginning the stocktake. If you don't trust the figure in your POS software, you can ask your accountant for an estimate.

Physically Counted Inventory Value

Article: Dravet Syndrome (DS) is also known as severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy. It is a rare early childhood intractable epileptic encephalopathy, which is associated with cognitive decline, pleomorphic seizure activity, and motor and behavioural abnormalities.

DS has been primarily associated with mutations in the gene SCN1A (Nav1.1 protein). It has been postulated that dysfunction of inhibitory neurons is associated with the development of DS. Nav1.1 protein product is the primary voltage-gated sodium channel in inhibitory neurons, and the impairment of Nav1.1 leads to unregulated transmission from gamma-aminobutyric acid-ergic (GABAergic) neurons.[1] 
Genetic studies have identified that duplications/deletions, missense mutations, nonsense mutations, frameshift mutations, or splice site mutations are responsible for the development of DS. Milder manifestations of DS might be observed due to missense mutations in SCN1A.
Other genes that have also been correlated to DS are SCN2A, SCN1B, SCN8A, PCDH19, STXBP1, GABRA1 and GABRG2.
DS evolves with age; following onset of seizure during infancy, neurodevelopmental delays progress to severe neurologic disability.
